# Abstract

> STROBE: Clear summary of study components; ISPOR-SMDM: Overview of model purpose

**Background**

Historical and projected smoking behaviour across Canadian populations is needed to evaluate tobacco control policies and to estimate the smoking-attributable disease burden. While the U.S. Smoking History Generator (SHG) supports cancer risk modelling, a pan-Canadian equivalent does not yet exist.

**Objectives**

This study aims to develop a Canadian Smoking Histories Model (CSHM) that reconstructs smoking patterns by birth cohort, sex, and province from 1965 to 2024, with projections to 2050. Specifically, we will: (1) estimate historical and current patterns of smoking initiation, cessation, and intensity; (2) assess regional and temporal variations across all provinces and territories; (3) project future trends under status quo conditions; and (4) provide an open-access, reproducible model for population health modelling.

**Methods**

Using harmonized data from more than 1 million respondents in the Canadian Community Health Survey (2001--2024), we will apply age-period-cohort models to estimate smoking initiation, cessation, and intensity. The cycles used for each analysis will depend on the variables and timing information available. Mortality-adjusted estimates using the MPoRT algorithm will address survival bias. Analyses will be stratified by sex, with estimates for each province and territory and projections to 2050.

**Expected Outcomes**

The model will be publicly accessible and used for policy evaluation and disease modelling in Canada, including projecting future smoking patterns and evaluating historic or proposed tobacco policy.

:::: {.section-body line-numbers="continuous"}

# 1. Background

Smoking behaviour varies across birth cohorts in ways that affect projections of tobacco-attributable disease and the evaluation of tobacco control policies in Canada. While smoking prevalence has declined since the mid-20th century, tobacco remains the leading cause of preventable disease and death in Canada, killing approximately 48,000 Canadians annually and costing over $11 billion per year in healthcare, lost productivity, and other costs [@HealthCanada_SmokingMortality_2024; @CSUCH_2023]. The smoking health burden is concentrated among lower-income and other equity-deserving populations, with lung cancer incidence nearly three times higher among Canadians with the lowest educational attainment [@mitra2015]. National trends hide differences between birth cohorts and provinces that follow from changing social norms and regional tobacco control measures.

The Smoking History Generator (SHG) framework, developed by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) CISNET Smoking Working Group, characterizes these patterns in the United States using Age-Period-Cohort (APC) models [@Holford_AJPM_2014]. This approach was adapted for Ontario [@Manuel_HR_2020], demonstrating that Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS) data can be used to reconstruct birth-cohort-specific smoking histories from 1965 to 2013. A pan-Canadian equivalent covering all provinces and territories has not yet been developed.

Three gaps motivate the development of a Canadian Smoking Histories Model (CSHM). First, tobacco control in Canada is set at both the national and regional levels, with inter-provincial variation in taxation, smoke-free legislation, and cessation support. Second, Canadian smoking initiation and cessation patterns differ from those in other countries, particularly in the timing of peak prevalence and the rate of decline among younger cohorts. Third, Canadian health policy models (e.g., OncoSim, POHEM, SimSmoke) rely on behaviour transition parameters from the 1994--2004 National Population Health Survey (NPHS), now over 20 years old, with no planned replacement [@hennessy2015; @gauvreau2017; @chaiton2021]. These parameters no longer reflect contemporary patterns, particularly among younger cohorts, immigrant populations, and lower-income groups.

This study will include an open-source framework for generating smoking histories across all Canadian jurisdictions. The CSHM will develop methods and infrastructure that build on those of other similar studies [@kopasker2023; @vasquezlavin2022]. The CSHM will also take advantage of the CCHS [@beland2002], which includes over 1.4 million respondents and annual data collection since 2001, making it a unique and unparalleled source of information.

# 2. Objectives

This study will develop a CSHM that describes smoking patterns by birth cohort, sex, and province from 1965 to 2024, with projections to 2050. Specifically, this study will:

> Note: the starting date (1965) may need revision based on model performance.

1.  **Estimate historical and current smoking parameters:** Reconstruct rates of smoking initiation, cessation, and intensity (cigarettes per day) by birth cohort (1890--2030) and sex for each province and territory.
2.  **Examine regional and temporal variations:** Analyse how smoking patterns have evolved across Canadian jurisdictions.
3.  **Project future smoking prevalence:** Model future trends in smoking prevalence and related parameters through 2050 under status quo policy conditions.
4.  **Develop an open-access model:** Create a publicly-accessible, reproducible R-based model that can be used and updated by researchers, policy analysts, and health system planners.

All analyses of smoking patterns, regional and temporal variation, and projections will be stratified by sex. The model will provide demographic and geographic estimates (by single year of age and birth cohort) to interface with existing population health models and support smoking projections and the evaluation of smoking preventive interventions, amongst other uses. Historical reporting will cover the period 1965--2024, with projections extending from 2025 to 2050. Where eligible transition data end earlier, estimates for the remaining reporting years will be identified as model extensions under the rules in section 3.4.3. Analysis will be conducted at the provincial level, with national estimates derived from aggregated provincial data.

# 3. Methods

## 3.1 Overall study design

This study uses a retrospective population-based simulation modelling approach to reconstruct and project smoking life-course trajectories for the Canadian population. We will use pooled cross-sectional data from the Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS) to estimate transition probabilities within an Age-Period-Cohort (APC) framework.

> STROBE: Study design; ISPOR-SMDM: Model type

The conceptual framework for the CSHM is structured as a discrete-time Markov state-transition model. The population is divided into three primary compartments: 

- **Never Smoker** (individuals who have smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes)
- **Current Smoker** (daily or occasional use, plus people who quit less than two years before the survey)
- **Former Smoker** (established smoker whose most recent quit has lasted $\ge$ 2 years at the survey).

Individuals transition between these states according to annual probabilities of **initiation** (from Never to Current) and **cessation** (from Current to Former). To estimate tobacco "dose", the Current Smoker compartment is further described by smoking intensity (cigarettes per day).

> ISPOR-SMDM: Model structure; STRESS: Conceptualization

The APC framework describes variation by age, calendar period and birth cohort, conditional on the identifying assumptions in section 3.4.3. The components do not identify the causes of that variation. This framework is used for three reasons:

1.  **Identifiability:** It addresses the fundamental APC identity ($cohort = period - age$) through explicit linear-trend constraints. Cubic splines describe curvature; the constraints state how the unidentified linear trend is allocated (section 3.4.3).
2.  **Historical reconstruction:** It back-calculates smoking rates for birth cohorts from the histories of current survivors.
3.  **Survival bias mitigation:** It will incorporate a separately specified mortality adjustment to address differences between the original birth cohorts and the people who survived to be surveyed (section 3.4.5).

> ISPOR-SMDM: Analytical approach; GATHER: Methods overview

## 3.2 Data sources

The primary data source for the CSHM is the Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS), a national cross-sectional survey conducted by Statistics Canada. The CCHS employs a multistage stratified cluster design [@beland2002]. Its annual component covered people aged 12 years and older through 2022 and people aged 18 years and older from 2023 onward, as described in the [Health Canada survey overview](https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/smoking-tobacco/surveys-statistics-research.html). Exclusions include people living on reserves, full-time members of the Canadian Forces and institutionalized populations. Planned coverage is 2001--2024. Inclusion in a particular analysis will depend on the age coverage, questions and variables available in each source file; including a cycle does not mean that every transition can be estimated through that year.

Each record requires a survey year for cohort assignment (birth cohort = survey year minus age). The first cycle (CCHS 1.1, collected from September 2000 to November 2001) remains assigned to 2001. Before reconstructing histories from other cycles, we will audit interview-year information in the Master files and PUMFs, particularly biennial releases, and document the assignment used for each source. A two-year file label alone does not identify a respondent's interview year. Any approximation required when interview year is unavailable must be agreed before fitting.

The study will use two distinct computing environments and data formats:

1.  **Development Environment (Public Use Microdata Files - PUMFs):** Initial model development, coding, and internal validation will be performed using PUMF data (cycles 2001--2022). These files contain about 1 million respondents and are used for the open-source implementation of the model. Continuous variables from the CCHS (e.g., age at initiation) are often provided as grouped response categories in PUMF data; midpoint-estimated pseudo-continuous values will be used only under the variable-specific rules in section 3.3. This is not a general rule for assigning exact timing to grouped quit durations.
2.  **Production Environment (Master Files):** The final model parameters will be estimated using CCHS Master Files (planned cycles 2001--2024) in authorized secure environments at Statistics Canada headquarters or Research Data Centres (RDCs). Master files retain more detailed responses than PUMFs where those responses were collected, but do not provide exact smoking-history timing in every cycle. We will document the available precision for age, initiation and cessation separately for each cycle. Grouped quit durations will follow the interval-constrained imputation approach in section 3.3, subject to verified source information and analysis eligibility.

The PUMF analysis will also provide independently reproducible estimates and a documented example for researchers adapting this approach outside Canada. It will not depend on access to Master data or Master-derived imputation parameters. Developing or calibrating PUMF imputation models or representative values using Master data is outside the scope of this study.

Secondary data sources for model calibration include:

3.  **Mortality data:** Age- and sex-specific mortality rates and life tables will be obtained from either Statistics Canada or the Canadian Human Mortality Database (CHMD) to support mortality adjustment (section 3.4.5). Either source is acceptable. We will seek national and provincial coverage from 1921 to the most recent available year and document the available years, ages and jurisdictions before analysis. The selected source, table identifiers, release version and any treatment of coverage gaps will be recorded with the analysis settings. Annual and multi-year estimates, and complete and abridged life tables, will be distinguished. Accepting either source does not assume that their coverage or estimates are identical. Access details are in Appendix C.

See [Appendix C: Data availability and computational environment] for data access procedures for each data source used in this study.

## 3.3 Exposure ascertainment

We will use the [`cchsflow` R package](https://github.com/Big-Life-Lab/cchsflow) (version 3.0) to harmonize smoking-related and other required variables across all CCHS cycles. This library provides a standardized metadata-driven approach to recoding survey responses into unified variables, which keeps coding consistent despite changes in survey questions over time.

Compared to the US National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) used in existing CISNET models, the CCHS provides more granular data on non-daily smoking. While the NHIS categorizes current smokers as smoking "every day" or "some days", the CCHS records more detail about occasional smokers. The NHIS has fewer annual respondents (approximately 27,000 for the NHIS versus 65,000 for the CCHS), but with an earlier start date for tobacco questions (1965 for NHIS versus 2001 for the CCHS) [@backinger2008]. The potential effect of these differences are more statistically stable earlier birth cohorts for NHIS, and greater statistical power for regional estimates using the CCHS.

Key smoking parameters to be extracted and harmonized include:

-   **Smoking status:** Classified into six categories: current daily, current occasional (former-daily), current occasional (never-daily), former-daily, former-occasional, and never smoker. Individuals who have smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in their lifetime will be classified as never smokers. The distinction between former-daily and never-daily occasional smokers allows for more precise characterization of the cessation process and tobacco "dose" over the life course. For the APC initiation and cessation models, these will be collapsed into Never, Current, and Former smokers.
-   **Age at initiation:** The CCHS captures the age at which the respondent first smoked a whole cigarette (`age_first_cigarette`) and the age at which they started smoking daily (`age_start_smoking`). In PUMF data, these values are derived from categorical responses using midpoint imputation. The lowest response category for these items on the PUMF data (e.g., ages 5 to 11, midpoint 8) is too coarse to date initiation events below that age, so the PUMF initiation model uses a floor of 13; an established smoker who reports starting below 13 is followed for cessation from age 15. The Master-file analysis uses exact ages with a floor of 8, and the two are reconciled there.
-   **Time since cessation:** The time since the respondent completely stopped smoking, distinguished from stopping daily smoking. We will preserve the most precise observed timing available within each source and retain grouped responses as intervals with their original category and source information. Grouped complete-cessation durations will be handled using interval-constrained multiple imputation, informed by available respondent information and prespecified distributional assumptions (section 3.4.2). The 2023 Master dictionary and the [2024 questionnaire](https://www23.statcan.gc.ca/imdb/p3Instr.pl?Function=assembleInstr&Item_Id=1532313) distinguish quits of less than one year, one to less than two years, two to less than three years, and three or more years. For substantive responses in these intervals, the two-year threshold is observed, although the exact cessation year is not. The complete-cessation paths are specified below. Other source intervals may cross the two-year threshold; smoking state and cessation timing will then be derived together in each completed dataset. Open-ended intervals require an explicit distribution and respondent-specific feasible upper bound; they will not be assigned a fixed three-year duration or an arbitrary midpoint in the primary analysis. The released 2024 field names and routing must be checked against the questionnaire before use; the documented 2023 mappings are specified below. Earlier exact responses will not be coarsened to match newer cycles. This decision does not extend interval imputation to other grouped variables or change the recent-PUMF age-specific eligibility restrictions in section 3.4.1.
-   **Smoking intensity:** The number of cigarettes smoked per day (CPD). Unlike the NHIS, the CCHS allows us to distinguish the intensity profiles of occasional smokers who were previously daily smokers from those who have always smoked occasionally.

The following sociodemographic covariates will also be extracted for use in imputation models, descriptive analyses, and mortality adjustment:

-   **Age:** Continuous age at survey (`DHHGAGE_cont`), derived from grouped categorical responses in PUMF using midpoint imputation; exact continuous age available in Master files.
-   **Sex:** Binary (`DHH_SEX`), available in all cycles.
-   **Racial-group covariate for imputation:** The proposed use is as an auxiliary imputation predictor, not a new stratification of the initiation or cessation models. The candidate is a binary white/non-white classification, as used in Manuel et al. (2020) [@Manuel_HR_2020]. Earlier cultural or racial-origin classifications and the newer visible-minority classification (`SDCDVVM`, Master files from 2019) are not interchangeable. The newer category "Not a visible minority" includes Indigenous and some multiple-group responses and cannot be relabelled "White". The binary candidate therefore applies directly only where a source identifies a White category. PUMF classifications through 2013--2014 label the other substantive category visible minority and retain a not-applicable category; in 2015--2018, the other substantive category explicitly includes Indigenous respondents. These mappings will be retained rather than treated as identical. The 2023 Master file also contains a raw White-response indicator (`PG_05A`), but it has a restricted question universe and permits a different classification from White alone. Using it requires an explicit rule for multiple responses and structural skips; it will not automatically replace the source classification. Indigenous identity will not be used as a separate category: its use requires engagement with First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities, which has not been undertaken for this analysis. The category mapping will document how Indigenous respondents are grouped under each source classification. The final terminology and mapping will be recorded before use.
-   **Immigration status and timing:** Immigration status (`SDCFIMM`) will be distinguished from country of birth. PUMF source categories combine immigrants and non-permanent residents from 2015--2016 onward; the 2022 PUMF reverses the source-code ordering. Harmonization will retain the source definition and correct code mapping. First arrival to live in Canada and becoming a landed immigrant can occur in different years. We will use directly reported first-arrival year where available within the question's eligible population and retain landed-immigrant year as a distinct measure. PUMF residence duration through 2017--2018 will retain its observed grouping, not an exact arrival year inferred from a representative value. Following the Canadian-population approach in Manuel et al. (2020) [@Manuel_HR_2020], years before arrival will not contribute Canadian person-years at risk or initiation events. Pre-arrival smoking history will still be retained where relevant to lifetime exposure. Where direct arrival is unavailable, the remaining decision is whether to use a specified approximation, interval reconstruction or restriction, with its sensitivity analysis. A landed-immigrant date cannot define entry for non-permanent residents.
-   **Education:** Three-category classification (less than high school, high school graduate, postsecondary graduate), used in imputation models. Note that education variables differ across cycles and between PUMF and Master files; harmonization will follow the `cchsflow` approach using `EDUDR03`.
-   **Province:** Used for provincial stratification and regional imputation models (`GEOGPRV`).


**Documented source definitions.** The following definitions come from the Statistics Canada dictionaries collected in [cchsflow-docs](https://github.com/Big-Life-Lab/cchsflow-docs), the PUMF DDI metadata in [cchsflow-data](https://github.com/Big-Life-Lab/cchsflow-data), and the 2024 questionnaire. Harmonization rules will be checked against these definitions, retaining the source field, question universe, response categories and missingness. A broad label such as years since immigration does not establish that the underlying concept is unchanged.

| Source | Field or response | Use in this study |
|---|---|---|
| Reviewed Master releases, 2001--2014 | `SDCA_3`, `SDCC_3`, `SDCE_3`, then `SDC_3`: first year coming to Canada to live | Direct arrival timing within each question's eligible population. Earlier routing does not cover every foreign-born respondent; for example, the 2001 question excludes Canadian citizens by birth. |
| Annual Master dictionaries, 2015--2021 | `SDC_IM4`: first year becoming a landed immigrant | Retain as landed year. The change in the reviewed questions occurs in 2015, not 2022. The derived `SDCDVRES` in this period uses landed-year information. |
| Master files, 2022--2023 | `IM_02`: first arrival; `IM_04`: first landed-immigrant year | Use direct arrival where observed; retain landed year separately. `SDCDVRES` derives from landed year even though direct arrival is available. |
| PUMFs, 2001--2017/2018 | Grouped residence duration: zero to nine years or 10 or more years; the later source labels give 10--121 years | Preserve the category and source concept. Values such as 4.5 or 15 years supplied by continuous harmonization are not observed arrival times. |
| Master file, 2023 | `SPU_10` for former occasional, never-daily smokers; `SPU_25`, `SPU_30` and `SPU_35` for former daily smokers | Use `SPU_10` for its eligible respondents. For former daily smokers, use the `SPU_25` interval only when `SPU_30` confirms that stopping daily smoking was complete cessation; otherwise use `SPU_35` when that follow-up is answered. Preserve missing gates and structural skips. |
| Questionnaire, 2024 | Arrival and landed-year questions; the same four complete-cessation intervals and daily-stop confirmation question | Questionnaire definitions are established. Verify released fields and routing before adding this cycle to the implementation. |

The documented complete-cessation intervals will be retained as lower and upper bounds, including an open upper interval. cchsflow's categorical mappings can support this representation; its continuous substitutes, including five years for three or more years, do not implement the study's interval-constrained imputation. Exact earlier responses will retain priority. For racial-group imputation, structural skips will not be recoded as non-white, and the residual visible-minority category will not be recoded as White. Where no comparable predictor is available, a common binary classification will not be manufactured by imputing across the classification change.

Inconsistent or biologically implausible responses (e.g., age at initiation greater than current age) will be identified during the data cleaning stage. Item non-response on smoking history parameters will be addressed using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), incorporating the sociodemographic and health-related predictors listed above. Observed grouped quit durations will retain their interval information in a separate, coordinated imputation procedure; they will not be relabelled as NA(b) or NA(c).

> STROBE: Statistical methods; GATHER: Data processing

## 3.4 Analytical approach

The CSHM uses a two-stage analytical framework. In the first stage, we estimate population-level smoking initiation and cessation rates from harmonized CCHS data using Age-Period-Cohort (APC) models. In the second stage, these estimated rates are used to simulate individual-level smoking histories for synthetic Canadian populations.

### 3.4.1 Smoking states and transition estimands

The model estimates transitions between three smoking states: **never**, **current**, and **former**. Each person is in exactly one state at each age. This is the framework of Holford et al. (2014) [@Holford_AJPM_2014], which has been applied in several jurisdictions, and of Manuel et al. (2020) [@Manuel_HR_2020] for Ontario using the CCHS. This study follows the Manuel et al. implementation because it uses the same survey.

A person enters the current state (initiation) at the age they smoked their first whole cigarette, provided they meet the study definition of an ever-smoker (i.e., smoked at least 100 cigarettes in their lifetime). A person leaves the current state (cessation) when they stop smoking completely; stopping daily smoking while continuing to smoke occasionally is not considered cessation. Starting to smoke daily and the number of cigarettes smoked per day are treated as characteristics of current smokers (section 3.4.4), not as separate transitions.

The APC models are estimated on person-years from the calendar year in which the earliest birth cohort (1920) reaches the initiation floor (1933 in the PUMF, where the floor is 13; 1928 in the Master files, where it is 8) to the last survey year. Every initiation event, therefore, has people at risk in the same age, period and cohort cell. A window that started later would keep the early events and remove the years at risk before them. Reported rates and reconstructed histories start in 1965; the earlier years are used for estimation only.

In the sensitivity analysis that starts cessation risk at first cigarette without the age-15 minimum, the cessation estimation window will also extend earlier if required to include eligible risk time. Its start is the earlier of the primary window start and the earliest eligible cessation person-year in that profile's national reference data. The initiation estimation window and the reporting window remain unchanged.

**Age and time ranges.** The reference studies use the same limits as those proposed for the CSHM. Holford et al. (2014) [@Holford_AJPM_2014] and Manuel et al. (2020) [@Manuel_HR_2020] set the probability of initiation before age 8 to zero and the probability of cessation before age 15 to zero. A quit is considered cessation only when it has lasted at least two years at the survey. Smoking histories will be followed to age 85: Holford et al. report up to age 99 but hold cessation rates constant at the age-85 level beyond age 85. This study maintains the two-year rule and the age-85 maximum: the CCHS reports ages up to 85 years in the PUMF, and rates for ages above 85 are held at the age-85 values.

The CSHM project differs from the reference studies in its PUMF initiation floor. Initiation is modelled from age 8 in the Master files but from age 13 in the PUMF, because the lowest PUMF age category (5 to 11 years) cannot place a first cigarette within a year (section 3.3); the PUMF response category floor is a data limitation; the method is the same in both files. Cessation risk begins at the later of age 15 and age at first whole cigarette. Cessation probability is set to zero before age 15, following the reference studies; respondents who start smoking after age 15 enter the cessation risk set when they start smoking.

The ranges of reported values (age at first cigarette, years since quitting, age at survey) come from the CCHS recoding rules in cchsflow (the variable-details worksheet) and are checked for each survey cycle; they describe what respondents can report; the analysis limits are stated above. The 2019--2020 and 2022 PUMF cycles report age in five broad groups, so age-specific estimation uses the 2001 to 2017--2018 cycles; the later cycles are used for cross-sectional prevalence only in PUMF analyses.

The model uses one-year steps and assigns each person at most one smoking period, from initiation to cessation. A person's cessation risk begins at the later of age 15 and the age they entered the current state. The CCHS records whether a respondent has smoked at least 100 cigarettes but does not record their age at the 100th cigarette. Among respondents who meet this criterion, age at first whole cigarette approximates the start of smoking. We do not impose a fixed one- or two-year delay after the first cigarette. The primary definition of cessation is the most recent quit that lasted at least two years. People who quit less than two years before the survey have not yet met this definition: they will be classified as current smokers at the time of survey, and in the cessation model they contribute time at risk up to their reported quit age, after which they are censored, with no cessation event recorded: this follows the Holford and Manuel implementations. When initiation and cessation are reported at the same whole-year age, the data cannot show which came first within the year. We will state the rule for these cases in the analysis specification before fitting the models, and we will run a prespecified sensitivity analysis that excludes or interval-censors them. The CCHS records one quit per person, so relapse cannot be modelled directly; its influence is examined in sensitivity analyses (section 3.5).

The target population is the Canadian household population covered by the CCHS. For immigrants, Canadian person-time begins at arrival, subject to the study's age and risk-set eligibility rules (section 3.3). Someone already smoking when they arrive can enter the cessation risk set but does not contribute a Canadian initiation event at arrival. Someone who quit before arrival does not contribute a Canadian cessation event for that earlier quit. Excluding pre-arrival Canadian risk time does not erase earlier exposure from a lifetime smoking history. The data-availability audit and any approximation for arrival timing must be completed before applying this rule. This defines entry into the reconstructed Canadian risk sets; the retrospective CCHS data do not observe every migration into or out of Canada. Respondents whose age at initiation is missing or implausible are included through multiple imputation (section 3.4.2 and Appendix D); they are not excluded, and they are not reclassified as never-smokers.

> ISPOR-SMDM: Model structure; STROBE: Variables

### 3.4.2 Data preparation and imputation

Analysis datasets will be produced through a standardized pipeline.

1.  **Cleaning:** Distribution checks and truncation of extreme values for continuous variables (e.g., smoking intensity). Harmonization across CCHS cycles using `cchsflow`.
2.  **Imputation:** Item non-response (don't know or refused; tagged NA(b)) on smoking status, initiation age, and cessation timing will be imputed with multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), with at least *m* = 5 imputations. The final number of imputations will be chosen so that the rate-table estimates are stable across repeated runs. This MICE procedure imputes item non-response; grouped quit durations follow the separate interval procedure below. Values that are missing by design are kept as missing: not applicable (NA(a), for example, initiation age for never-smokers) and not asked in that cycle (NA(c)). Imputation follows the structure of the smoking questions. Where a person's smoking status is itself missing, status is imputed first; initiation age and quit timing are then imputed only if the imputed status makes those questions applicable, using the other smoking-history variables as predictors. Ordering rules (first cigarette no later than cessation; cessation no later than survey age) are applied within the imputation procedure, not corrected afterward. The imputation model includes the survey design variables (cycle, sampling weight), the sociodemographic variables (age, sex, province, education), and the smoking-history variables, making it at least as detailed as the analysis models. It also includes auxiliary variables (marital status, alcohol use, body mass index, self-rated general and mental health, life stress, community belonging, chronic conditions, and physical activity), which improve imputation and describe the study base for planned related studies. Derived variables such as pack-years are recalculated from the imputed component variables rather than imputed directly. Every completed dataset is carried through person-year expansion and model fitting, and estimates are pooled across imputations (section 3.5). The full specification, including the diagnostic and sensitivity plan, is in [Appendix D: Missing data and imputation plan](appendix-imputation.qmd).
3.  **Descriptive statistics:** Baseline characteristics will be reported pre-imputation (Table 1a), which discloses the amount and type of missing data, and post-imputation (Table 1b), averaged across the *m* completed datasets. Both tables present unweighted n with survey-weighted percentages (and weighted median/IQR for continuous variables) -- the unweighted n reflects the information content of each cell, while the weighted statistics describe the population; a fully unweighted variant is provided in the appendix. Table 1 will include stratification for sex and survey year. Descriptive statistics will be examined for potential discontinuities across CCHS design eras (2001--2005, 2007--2014, 2015--2021, 2022+), which reflect major changes to the survey frame, recruitment, and collection mode [@gagne2017; @backinger2008]. We will examine 2020 separately where annual observations can be identified, comparing smoking prevalence and respondent characteristics with adjacent years. Comparisons spanning the 2023 age-coverage change will use common age ranges, separately from descriptions of each cycle's full sample. Although smoking variables can be harmonized across cycles, changes to the sampling frame and mode may introduce measurement differences that are not fully correctable through harmonization alone [@chen2020joinpoint]. These descriptive checks do not establish a causal effect of survey redesign. Whether to refit the models excluding 2020 remains a decision for review; a formal discontinuity test is not prespecified in this draft.

**Grouped quit-duration imputation.** In addition to item-non-response imputation, we will draw plausible complete-cessation durations within each respondent's observed interval. The draws must respect interval endpoint conventions and the ordering of initiation, complete cessation and interview. Bounds will use the available respondent history; an analysis age floor will not be used to erase an earlier reported quit. Impossible combinations will be flagged for review rather than clipped or silently assigned a midpoint. The source response and interval will remain unchanged alongside the imputed duration.

Within each completed dataset, we will derive age and year at cessation, the modelled smoking state and the applicable risk history from the same draw. A qualifying quit is dated at cessation, not two years later. Quits shorter than the threshold retain the current-state classification and censoring rule in section 3.4.1. The interval procedure will be coordinated with item-non-response imputation where missing smoking history or gate responses affect eligibility or bounds. Every completed dataset will proceed through the analysis; source-category and missingness summaries in Table 1a will remain based on the observed data.

Before fitting, we will record the primary distribution, conditioning variables, open-ended interval treatment, number of completed datasets, and rules for combining item-non-response, interval-imputation and survey uncertainty. These details require simulation checks and a dated specification; selecting interval-constrained multiple imputation does not establish that any particular distribution is adequate. Master-informed PUMF imputation is excluded (section 3.2).

### 3.4.3 Age-period-cohort modelling

Three separate APC models will be fitted by sex (men and women) to characterize smoking life-course trajectories: one for initiation, one for cessation, and one for smoking intensity (cigarettes per day). The primary analysis produces national estimates stratified by sex, as well as separate estimates for each province and territory.

The initiation and cessation models use natural cubic splines to describe how rates change with age, calendar period, and birth cohort. Because period equals age plus cohort, the data cannot distinguish the straight-line (linear) trends in age, period, and cohort: any amount of linear trend can be shifted from one to the other without changing the fitted rates [@Holford_SM_2006]. We therefore state the linear-trend constraint separately for each transition. For initiation, the period linear trend is set to zero; for cessation, the cohort linear trend is set to zero. Age retains its linear term in both models. These choices follow the transition-specific constraints in Meza et al. (2023) [@Meza_AJPM_2023]. Setting a linear trend to zero retains the curvature of that component. It does not remove the period or cohort term, or establish a causal interpretation.

We fit the model in terms of quantities that the data can estimate: age-related shape, period and cohort curvature, and net drift. The alternative allocation of the linear trend is a sensitivity analysis (section 3.5). With otherwise equivalent models, changing this allocation should preserve fitted probabilities on observed age-period-cohort combinations. Projections can differ because they hold individual components constant outside the observed range.

For reproducibility, the proposed Canadian decomposition defines curvature as orthogonal to the constant and linear terms on an equally weighted, single-year grid between each component's boundary knots. Each grid is centred at its midpoint. This convention defines which linear component is set to zero and will be saved with the fitted model; deleting an arbitrary spline column does not implement it.

**Proposed primary knot locations.** The locations below adapt the transition-specific age and cohort knots in the supplementary methods of Salgado et al. (2024), a recent smoking-history study with Meza [@Salgado_LRHA_2024]. That study used an age-cohort initiation model and an APC cessation model. Our initiation period term and the additional 2010 period knot are proposed Canadian adaptations for the longer CCHS series. These choices are prespecified candidates for the primary analysis; they have not been shown to be optimal for Canadian data.

| Transition and component | Proposed interior knots |
|---|---|
| Initiation: age, Master files | 10, 12, 14, 17, 21, 24, 27, 50, 60 |
| Initiation: age, PUMF | 14, 17, 21, 24, 27, 50, 60 |
| Cessation: age | 30, 40, 50, 60 |
| Initiation and cessation: period | 1940, 1960, 1980, 2000, 2010 |
| Initiation: cohort | 1940, 1950, 1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 1995 |
| Cessation: cohort | 1930, 1940, 1950, 1960, 1970, 1980, 1990 |

These are explicitly **interior** knots in the Canadian model, with boundary knots specified separately. Adopting published numerical locations under this convention does not reproduce another study's spline basis. The PUMF initiation list excludes ages 10 and 12 because its initiation floor is 13.

Age boundary knots are 8 and 85 for Master-file initiation, 13 and 85 for PUMF initiation, and 15 and 85 for primary cessation. For period, the boundaries are the earliest and latest eligible person-years in the national reference data for that transition and source. For cohort, the lower boundary is 1920 and the upper boundary is the latest birth cohort represented in those eligible data. Eligibility follows the declared risk-set and survey-variable availability rules; it does not depend on whether a cell contains an event. These rules are resolved into numerical boundaries once for each source and analysis profile, before sex-specific and regional model fitting, and held fixed across imputations and bootstrap replicates. In held-out-cycle validation, they are resolved separately within each training split, without using the held-out observations. We will report the resolved values and the weighted and unweighted support by age, period and cohort. Recent cohort coverage does not imply that the full smoking history of those cohorts has been observed.

Projection rules are separate from the constraints that identify the fitted model. For status quo projections, period effects are held at the latest eligible period for each transition, and cohort effects are held at the boundary values for cohorts before 1920 or after the latest eligible cohort. The 1985 upper cohort cutoff inherited from the Ontario study is not retained for this expanded series. These extension rules apply when predicting outside the declared range; they do not cap the period or cohort values used to fit the model. Predictions for age-period-cohort combinations without observed support are labelled separately, including combinations inside the marginal boundaries.

The spline basis (interior and boundary knots, centring constants, and the linear-trend constraint) is part of the model definition. The basis built for fitting is saved and reused for every prediction and projection; it is never rebuilt from the prediction grid. Before any fitted model is used, we check its rank, convergence and estimability. Unsupported knots or an unidentified model stop the analysis for review rather than silently changing the specification. Any subsequent amendment to the primary settings will be recorded before the final analysis. The intensity specification will be reviewed separately under section 3.4.4; it will not inherit a transition model's knots by default.

### 3.4.4 Smoking intensity analysis

Daily and occasional smoking remain characteristics within the three-state model, not additional initiation or cessation transitions. We will retain the more detailed smoking categories for descriptive and intensity analyses, including the distinction between occasional smokers who previously smoked daily and those who did not.

We will use a dual approach to characterize smoking intensity (cigarettes per day; CPD):

1.  **Simple descriptives:** We will first calculate mean CPD and intensity distributions by age, sex, survey year and daily/occasional smoking category, with the denominator stated for each estimate. This descriptive analysis will identify temporal and cohort differences, including whether the Canadian patterns resemble those reported in Brazil [@Tam_AJPM_2023]. Reported current consumption will be distinguished from modelled smoking state: people who have quit for less than two years remain in the modelled current state but will not be assigned positive current consumption solely because of that classification.
2.  **APC intensity model:** We will fit an APC model to estimate expected CPD by birth cohort for use in exposure and pack-year reconstruction. Before fitting, we will specify the outcome distribution, daily/occasional treatment, spline settings and projection rule with the study team, including Rafael. For occasional smokers, the conversion to average cigarettes per calendar day will depend on the frequency and quantity questions available in each cycle; a common conversion has not yet been selected. Assumptions used to reconstruct earlier intensity and pack-years from survey-time reports will be stated separately from the observed responses. The intensity model will not inherit the initiation or cessation specification by default.

### 3.4.5 Mortality adjustment

To address survival bias, whereby ever-smokers have lower likelihood of survival to the survey date than never-smokers, we will apply mortality adjustments using the Mortality Population Risk Tool (MPoRT) [@Manuel_HR_2020]. MPoRT weights are adjusted for age, sex, smoking status, years since quitting, and immigration status. For each respondent, the one-year probability of death for each historical year up to the survey date is calculated; the survival-bias weight is the proportion of ever-smokers who would have died before the survey date. With this adjustment the reconstructed historical prevalence reflects the original population rather than only the survivors, following the approach of Manuel et al. (2020) [@Manuel_HR_2020].

The exact form of the adjustment will be documented and reviewed before it is implemented. The main open question is where the adjustment enters the calculation: as an adjustment to each respondent's weight before the APC models are fitted (as described above), or as a correction to the fitted transition probabilities afterward (as in the original Ontario code). The two approaches do not necessarily yield the same answer, and whichever is chosen must apply the correction only once. Before use, the adjustment will be checked in three ways: predicted deaths by age, sex, and calendar year compared with Canadian life tables; the size and stability of the adjustment factors, with limits set in advance; and recovery of known rates from simulated cohorts in which smokers die at higher rates (section 3.5). MPoRT remains the primary method if it passes these checks [@Manuel_HR_2020]. Until an adjustment is in place, unadjusted results are labelled as estimates among survivors and are not presented as birth-cohort smoking histories.

A sensitivity analysis will be conducted using the Peto approach -- a constant mortality risk ratio by smoking status -- consistent with the original Holford et al. (2014) US implementation [@Holford_AJPM_2014]. This quantifies the influence of the mortality adjustment method on historical prevalence estimates.

> ISPOR-SMDM: Model structure; GATHER: Statistical methods

CCHS sampling weights (`WTS_M` in Master files; equivalent PUMF weights) are applied throughout the analysis. In descriptive analyses, weights are used with the `{survey}` package to produce design-based estimates with bootstrap variance estimation. In the APC models, sampling weights are used as regression weights in the binomial logistic regression, following the pseudo-likelihood approach of Manuel et al. (2020) [@Manuel_HR_2020]: weighted events and weighted person-years are summed within each age-period-cohort cell before model fitting. How the mortality adjustment combines with these weights depends on the derivation described above. If the adjustment is applied to respondent weights before fitting, the survey weight and the mortality adjustment are combined into a single weight, so that each is applied once. If the adjustment is applied to the fitted probabilities afterward, the regression uses the survey weights alone.

### 3.4.6 Projections to 2050

Estimated initiation, cessation, and intensity rates will be extrapolated to 2050. The projection engine will support the following scenarios:

-  **Status quo scenarios:** Initiation and cessation period effects are held constant at their latest eligible periods, with cohort extensions as specified in section 3.4.3. Age patterns continue as cohorts age. This is a conditional projection under fixed period effects, rather than an estimate of the consequences of maintaining particular policies.
-  **Continued period trend:** A separate scenario may extend recent period trends. Its trend window, extrapolation rule and limits will require a further protocol decision before it is run. It will not replace the primary status quo scenario. The intensity projection rule will be specified with the intensity model.

### 3.4.7 Provincial and territorial estimates

Separate APC models will be estimated for each province and territory, stratified by sex. Provinces and territories with limited sample sizes may require pooled CCHS cycles or adjusted model constraints for stable estimates. The simulation engine runs on individual CCHS respondents, which gives regional projections that are consistent with national aggregates.

> GATHER: Statistical methods; ISPOR-SMDM: Subgroup analysis

## 3.5 Model validation and uncertainty analysis

The model will be validated through:

1.  **Internal validation:** Comparing smoking prevalence reconstructed by the model with prevalence observed in the CCHS. Some survey cycles or subsamples will be held out of model fitting, so that this comparison is not made against the data to which the model was fitted. We will also check recall consistency: whether the same birth cohort reports a consistent smoking history across different survey cycles.

> ISPOR-SMDM: Internal validation; STRESS: Validation - internal

2.  **External validation:** None in this version. Other surveys have their own measurement and response errors. For example, smoking prevalence in the CCHS is typically higher than in tobacco-specific surveys, likely reflecting the CCHS's broader sampling frame and higher response rate rather than measurement error. Comparing sources without a model of the errors in each would mislead more than it would validate, and these errors are often overlooked. We therefore defer the comparison. A future version may use the measurement error estimated from Canadian Health Measures Survey biomarkers (item 4) to adjust the estimates rather than only compare them. Validating within the CCHS cannot detect bias that affects the entire survey; we acknowledge this limitation.

> ISPOR-SMDM: External validation; STRESS: Validation - external

3.  **Uncertainty analysis:** In the Master-file analysis, uncertainty is estimated with the CCHS bootstrap replicate weights [@StatCan_CCHS_UserGuide_2022; @Rao_SM_1992]. Each replicate reweights whole respondents, so a respondent's full reconstructed history is kept together. The replicate estimates are repeated within each completed imputation dataset, and the variance from the survey design is combined with the variance between imputations using a rule set that is specified in advance and checked by simulation. Uncertainty is carried through to the published rate tables and projections, not reported only for model coefficients. The PUMFs do not include replicate weights or design variables. For analyses of those files, we use a bootstrap that resamples respondents, approximating the survey design as much as the file allows, and we check the results against Statistics Canada's published approximate coefficients of variation for descriptive estimates. All intervals from PUMF analyses are labelled approximate; the definitive intervals come from the Master-file analysis. Simulated replicate weights, generated with the public MockData package, are used to test the replicate-weight code in the public repository. They test only the code; results based on them are never reported.

> ISPOR-SMDM: Uncertainty analysis; STRESS: Sensitivity analysis

4.  **Sensitivity testing and measurement error:**
    -   **Grouped quit durations:** Compare the primary interval-imputation specification with prespecified alternative within-interval distributions and open-ended interval assumptions. Include a transparent fixed representative-value benchmark with its values and bounds declared. Compare cessation probabilities, reconstructed smoking prevalence and projections, using thresholds for substantively meaningful differences agreed before inspecting the comparisons. Distinguish variation across distributional assumptions from uncertainty within a specified imputation model. Independently estimated PUMF and Master results will be compared over common populations, cycles and reporting support where feasible; Master results will not be used to select or tune PUMF imputations. Agreement cannot rule out response or recall biases shared by both sources.
    -   **Smoking cessation length:** Repeat the cessation analysis with a one-year smoking-cessation threshold. This analysis follows a sensitivity analysis in Manuel et al. (2020) and will compare cessation probabilities, reconstructed smoking prevalence, and projections with the primary two-year definition.
    -   **Starting age for cessation risk:** Repeat the analysis with cessation risk beginning at age at first whole cigarette, without the age-15 minimum. Retain the requirement of at least two years since quitting and compare cessation probabilities, reconstructed smoking prevalence, and projections with the primary analysis.
    -   **Self-report bias:** Assessing the impact of misclassification using Simulation Extrapolation (SIMEX) informed by CHMS biomarker (cotinine) data. Corrected parameters will be propagated through the simulation engine to quantify the impact on final projections. Consideration will also be given to sensitivity testing for measurement differences attributable to CCHS survey design changes across eras.
    -   **Recall bias and relapse:** Quantifying the effect of the CCHS single-event history (relapse cycles are not recorded) by comparing net transition rates against observed longitudinal dynamics in the National Population Health Survey (NPHS) panel.
    -   **Back-casting comparison:** Reconstructing smoking prevalence for the 1994--2000 period and comparing against observed NPHS data -- interpreted as a consistency check rather than validation, since NPHS carries its own frame and measurement error structure (see §3.5 item 2).
    -   **Model specification:** Run three named sensitivity profiles, each compared with the primary analysis. The `ontario_knot_locations` profile replaces the interior-knot lists with Ontario-reference locations: initiation age 10, 15, 20, 50 and 60 (omitting 10 in the PUMF); cessation age 30, 40, 50 and 60; period 1940, 1950, 1960, 1970 and 1980 for both transitions; initiation cohort 1930, 1940, 1945, 1950, 1955, 1960, 1965, 1970, 1975 and 1980; and cessation cohort 1940, 1950, 1960, 1970 and 1980. It retains the primary boundary rules, linear-trend constraints and projection rules, so it compares knot locations without claiming to reproduce the Ontario analysis. The `without_2010_period_knot` profile removes only the 2010 interior period knot from both transitions. The `alternate_linear_trend` profile sets the cohort linear trend to zero for initiation and the period linear trend to zero for cessation, retaining all primary knots and boundaries. We will compare transition probabilities, reconstructed prevalence, held-out-cycle performance and projections to 2050, with particular attention to recent cohorts and small jurisdictions. These comparisons assess dependence on prespecified assumptions; they do not automatically select a replacement primary model.
    -   **Spline implementation check:** Compare natural-spline and restricted-cubic-spline implementations with matched interior knots, boundary knots, centring and linear-trend constraints. They describe the same function space under equivalent specifications, so fitted probabilities should agree within a declared numerical tolerance. This is a software check, not a separate scientific sensitivity analysis.
    -   **Mortality adjustment method:** The primary analysis uses the MPoRT algorithm for mortality adjustment. We will conduct a sensitivity analysis using the Peto approach (a constant mortality risk ratio by smoking status), consistent with the original Holford et al. (2014) US implementation, to quantify the influence of the mortality adjustment method on historical prevalence estimates.
    -   **Vaping transitions:** Testing alternative assumptions for younger cohorts regarding the relationship between vaping initiation and subsequent smoking (gateway, displacement, or common liability scenarios).

> STROBE: Potential bias; STRESS: Sensitivity analysis

## 3.6 Computational methods

The CSHM is implemented in R (version 4.2+) using a reproducible pipeline architecture. See [Appendix C: Data availability and computational environment] for full details of the software environment, package dependencies, and code availability.

Analysis choices will be recorded in `config.yml`, separately from computing-environment profiles. A named `primary` analysis profile will define transition- and source-specific knots, boundary rules, linear-trend constraints, estimation and reporting limits, and projection rules. Named sensitivity profiles will inherit the primary settings and declare only their intended changes. The one-year quit-period and first-cigarette cessation-entry analyses will use separate profiles; changing those rules will rebuild the relevant smoking states and risk sets as well as refit the models. The first-cigarette profile will lower the cessation age boundary below 15 where required to include the earliest eligible entry age in its national reference data, and extend the cessation estimation window as described in section 3.4.1. Other analyses in section 3.5 will use the same configuration approach once their methods are fully specified; a configuration option alone does not establish that a method has been implemented.

The grouped quit-duration specification will use the same configuration approach. Settings will record source- and cycle-specific interval mappings, endpoint conventions, distributional assumptions, conditioning variables, feasible-bound rules, imputation counts, random seeds and named sensitivity profiles. Source mappings will be separate from the general imputation method to support adaptation to other surveys. No Master-derived parameters will be required for PUMF execution. Only verified mappings and implemented, validated methods may be selected.

The pipeline will validate the complete resolved settings before fitting. It will reject unknown or conflicting options, invalid knot and boundary combinations, and requests for methods that are not implemented. Each run will save its profile name, resolved numerical settings, configuration identifier, software revision and input-data version alongside the fitted basis and diagnostics. Outputs and cached results will be distinguished by analysis profile and configuration identifier so that primary and sensitivity runs cannot overwrite or reuse incompatible results.

> STRESS: Implementation details; ISPOR-SMDM: Computational methods

# 4. Expected outcomes

The primary output of this study is the CSHM: a validated, open-source tool for population health modelling.

Specific outputs include:

1.  **Annual rate tables:** A complete set of estimated rates for smoking initiation, cessation, and intensity by single year of age, birth cohort (1890--2030), sex, and province. These will cover the historical reporting period (1965--2024) and future projections (2025--2050). Tables will identify source- and transition-specific estimation limits and any model extensions within the reporting period.
2.  **Total smoking burden estimates:** Annual estimates of the total number of cigarettes smoked in Canada by calendar year, derived by combining smoking prevalence, intensity (cigarettes per day), and population counts. This aggregate measure provides a direct indicator of national tobacco exposure over time and can be used to contextualize tobacco policy impacts and project future cigarette consumption.

3.  **Individual-level smoking histories:** Synthetic birth-cohort-specific smoking histories will be generated directly from the estimated APC rate tables, following the approach of Manuel et al. (2020) [@Manuel_HR_2020] and Holford et al. (2014) [@Holford_AJPM_2014]. For each birth cohort, the probability of being a current, former, or never smoker at each age is derived by combining the initiation and cessation rate tables with the mortality adjustment. These histories provide the inputs needed for microsimulation models of tobacco-attributable disease burden in Canada.
4.  **Open-source repository:** All R code, metadata worksheets, and documentation will be made publicly available on GitHub so that the analysis can be reproduced and updated as new CCHS cycles are released.

> GATHER: Access to data and analytics; STRESS: Implementation details

5.  **Interactive online platform:** A web-based dashboard (built using R Shiny) will allow users to visualize smoking trends by province and cohort, download rate tables, and compare projection scenarios.

> GATHER: Results publication; ISPOR-SMDM: Reporting

The CSHM will provide input to established Canadian health policy models, such as OncoSim (cancer) and POHEM (chronic disease), to support the evaluation of tobacco control policies and the estimation of smoking-attributable disease burden (e.g., cancer, cardiovascular disease, and dementia) at national and provincial levels. This follows the model-based policy evaluation approach used in other jurisdictions [@Meza_J_2021].

> ISPOR-SMDM: Model application; CHEERS: Model-based evaluation

# 5. Timeline and resources

## Governance and collaboration

The CSHM is co-led by the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute, the BC Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (BCCDC), and Statistics Canada's Health Analysis and Modelling Division. The core modelling team is responsible for analytical decisions. Partner representatives, including the Canadian Partnership Against Cancer, will review key milestone outputs and the final model prior to dissemination. Roles and responsibilities are documented in the project repository.

> ISPOR-SMDM: Project management; STRESS: Project planning

## Prespecification

This protocol records the prespecified analysis plan and identifies methods that still require a study-team decision. Items explicitly marked for review, including the intensity specification and the distributional and uncertainty-combination details for grouped quit-duration imputation, are not finalized methods and will be resolved in a dated revision before their analyses are run. Any deviations from the prespecified plan will be documented in the repository changelog and reported in the methods of any resulting publications.

## Key milestones

| Phase | Activities | Environment |
|---|---|---|
| Data preparation | CCHS harmonization, variable QC, descriptive tables | PUMF |
| Model development | APC model fitting, spline tuning, sensitivity analyses | PUMF |
| Master-file analysis | Replication using the most detailed available responses; cycle-specific timing checks | Statistics Canada headquarters or RDC |
| Validation | Internal validation (held-out cycles, recall consistency); NPHS back-casting comparison; SIMEX | PUMF + secure Master-file environment |
| Dissemination | Open-source release; manuscript submission; Shiny dashboard | Public |

## Resource and access considerations

This study involves the secondary analysis of de-identified survey data. Analysis of CCHS Master Files will be conducted in authorized secure environments at Statistics Canada headquarters or Research Data Centres, following all protocols for data privacy and disclosure control. No individual-level data that could identify respondents will be released. The use of PUMF data for model development is subject to the Statistics Canada Open Licence agreement.

## Appendix C: Data availability and computational environment {#appendix-c-data-availability}

The following sections describe access to the CCHS and mortality inputs, and to NHIS data for any supplementary descriptive comparisons.

## Canadian Community Health Survey -- Public Use Microdata Files (PUMF)

The CCHS PUMF files are publicly accessible and available without special permissions or restricted access. PUMF files can be downloaded from the [Ontario Data Documentation, Extraction Service and Infrastructure (ODESI)](https://odesi.ca) and directly from [Statistics Canada](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/en/catalogue/82M0013X). The PUMF files contain de-identified data and are released under the Statistics Canada Open Licence. These files are used for model development and the open-source implementation of the CSHM.

## Canadian Community Health Survey -- Master Files

The CCHS Master Files, used for the production model estimates, will be analysed by authorized team members at Statistics Canada headquarters or Research Data Centres (RDCs). External researchers must obtain access through the applicable Statistics Canada approval process; headquarters analysis requires the corresponding internal authorization. Both settings provide access to confidential microdata under the confidentiality provisions of the *Statistics Act* and apply Statistics Canada's privacy and disclosure controls. Master files retain detailed responses that may be grouped in the PUMF, but precision depends on what was collected in each cycle. They cannot recover exact cessation timing from questions that recorded only grouped durations (section 3.3). Further information about RDC access procedures, eligibility, and application requirements is available on the [Statistics Canada website](https://www.statcan.gc.ca/en/microdata/data-centres).

## Mortality rates and life tables

Mortality inputs may come from [Statistics Canada life tables](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1310011401) or the [Canadian Human Mortality Database](http://www.bdlc.umontreal.ca/CHMD). Statistics Canada provides complete life tables for Canada and most provinces, with separate abridged tables for Prince Edward Island and the territories. The chosen series and its age, geographic and historical coverage will be documented before analysis, together with download date and release version. Access to these aggregate mortality inputs does not require access to confidential CCHS Master records.

## US National Health Interview Survey (NHIS)

The NHIS is the data source for the US Smoking History Generator. It is not used to validate the CSHM in this version (section 3.5); descriptive comparisons of Canadian and US cohort patterns may be reported. The NHIS is conducted by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). Public-use NHIS data files are freely available without special permissions and can be downloaded directly from the [NCHS website](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/data-questionnaires-documentation.htm). The public-use files contain de-identified data. For researchers requiring access to more detailed data not available in the public-use files, the NCHS Research Data Center offers access to restricted-use files subject to an application process and strict confidentiality protocols. Further information is available at <https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.htm>.

Any NHIS descriptive comparison remains supplementary and is not part of the primary validation analysis.

> GATHER: Data access; STROBE: Ethics

## Computational environment

The CSHM is implemented in the R programming environment (version 4.2+). The project architecture uses a reproducible data science workflow:

-   **Pipeline management:** The `{targets}` R package manages the dependency graph and recomputes only the targets whose inputs have changed.
-   **Environment management:** The `{renv}` package records the exact versions of all R packages and keeps the software environment the same across development, production, and the Statistics Canada RDC environment.
-   **Harmonization:** The `{cchsflow}` package (version 3.0) harmonizes survey data across CCHS cycles.

All code will be hosted on GitHub under an MIT licence. The repository will include full documentation, metadata worksheets, and instructions for replication on both PUMF and Master file environments.

> STRESS: Implementation details; GATHER: Access to data and analytics

## Appendix D: Missing data and imputation plan

The detailed missing-data specification -- the tagged-NA taxonomy, the `where`-matrix MICE design, cycle-level absence handling, the Table 1a/1b weighting presentation, and the four-phase diagnostic and sensitivity-analysis plan -- is maintained as a standalone document: [Appendix D: Missing data and imputation plan](appendix-imputation.qmd). It adapts the DemPoRTv2 imputation assessment framework with improvements developed for this study.

> STROBE: Statistical methods (missing data); GATHER: Data processing
